claim: Animals that feed on mobile prey have evolved a repertoire of anatomical features and behavioural strategies to maximize capture success.
source: Animals that feed on mobile prey have evolved a repertoire of anatomical features and behavioural strategies to maximize capture success (Lima, 2002), matched by prey in an evolutionary arms race in their attempts to avoid capture (Randall et al., 1995; Walker et al., 2005; Cortez, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lima (2002), Randall et al. (1995), Walker et al. (2005), and Cortez (2011).

claim: Prey have evolved features and strategies matched to predators in an evolutionary arms race in their attempts to avoid capture.
source: Animals that feed on mobile prey have evolved a repertoire of anatomical features and behavioural strategies to maximize capture success (Lima, 2002), matched by prey in an evolutionary arms race in their attempts to avoid capture (Randall et al., 1995; Walker et al., 2005; Cortez, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Randall et al. (1995), Walker et al. (2005), and Cortez (2011).

claim: Numerous authors have examined strategies for both predators and prey in predator-prey interactions.
source: Numerous authors have examined strategies for both predators and prey in such interactions (Weihs and Webb, 1984; Domenici et al., 2011), with a particular wealth of literature on animals operating in air (Warrick, 1998; Hedenström and Rosén, 2001) and water (Domenici, 2001) with considerations ranging from turn capacity (Fish, 1999), through random turning behaviour by prey (Jones et al., 2011; Combes et al., 2012) to speed accuracy tradeoffs during decision making (Chittka et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Weihs and Webb (1984), Domenici et al. (2011), and others.

claim: There is a particular wealth of literature on predator-prey interactions in animals operating in air and water.
source: Numerous authors have examined strategies for both predators and prey in such interactions (Weihs and Webb, 1984; Domenici et al., 2011), with a particular wealth of literature on animals operating in air (Warrick, 1998; Hedenström and Rosén, 2001) and water (Domenici, 2001) with considerations ranging from turn capacity (Fish, 1999), through random turning behaviour by prey (Jones et al., 2011; Combes et al., 2012) to speed accuracy tradeoffs during decision making (Chittka et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature on aerial (Warrick, 1998; Hedenström and Rosén, 2001) and aquatic (Domenici, 2001) predator-prey interactions.

claim: Considerations in predator-prey interactions range from turn capacity, through random turning behaviour by prey, to speed accuracy tradeoffs during decision making.
source: Numerous authors have examined strategies for both predators and prey in such interactions (Weihs and Webb, 1984; Domenici et al., 2011), with a particular wealth of literature on animals operating in air (Warrick, 1998; Hedenström and Rosén, 2001) and water (Domenici, 2001) with considerations ranging from turn capacity (Fish, 1999), through random turning behaviour by prey (Jones et al., 2011; Combes et al., 2012) to speed accuracy tradeoffs during decision making (Chittka et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fish (1999), Jones et al. (2011), Combes et al. (2012), and Chittka et al. (2009).

claim: Such considerations appear less well developed in terrestrial, cursorial interactions.
source: Such considerations appear less well developed in terrestrial, cursorial interactions with, in particular, no discussion of how varying mass between parties might affect strategy, although this has been examined in the aquatic literature (Domenici, 2001).
evidence: Based on the authors' assessment of the literature and comparison to aquatic studies.

claim: There is no discussion of how varying mass between parties might affect strategy in terrestrial, cursorial interactions.
source: Such considerations appear less well developed in terrestrial, cursorial interactions with, in particular, no discussion of how varying mass between parties might affect strategy, although this has been examined in the aquatic literature (Domenici, 2001).
evidence: Based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: How varying mass between parties might affect strategy has been examined in the aquatic literature.
source: Such considerations appear less well developed in terrestrial, cursorial interactions with, in particular, no discussion of how varying mass between parties might affect strategy, although this has been examined in the aquatic literature (Domenici, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Domenici (2001).

claim: Elliot et al. (1977) provided a conceptual model for prey acquisition by terrestrial carnivores describing four major elements: the search, the stalk, the attack, and the subdue.
source: Elliot et al., (1977) provided a conceptual model for prey acquisition by terrestrial carnivores describing four major elements; the search, the stalk, the attack, and the subdue.
evidence: Supported by citation to Elliot et al. (1977).

claim: The attack is the most power-demanding element of prey acquisition by terrestrial carnivores.
source: Of these, the attack is the most power-demanding (Williams et al., 2014), typically involving complex high speed manoeuvres (Van Damme and Van Dooren, 1999; Kane and Zamani, 2014), underpinned by apparently complicated behavioural options for both predators and prey (Estes and Goddard, 1967; Wilson et al., 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Williams et al. (2014).

claim: The attack typically involves complex high speed manoeuvres.
source: Of these, the attack is the most power-demanding (Williams et al., 2014), typically involving complex high speed manoeuvres (Van Damme and Van Dooren, 1999; Kane and Zamani, 2014), underpinned by apparently complicated behavioural options for both predators and prey (Estes and Goddard, 1967; Wilson et al., 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Van Damme and Van Dooren (1999) and Kane and Zamani (2014).

claim: The attack is underpinned by apparently complicated behavioural options for both predators and prey.
source: Of these, the attack is the most power-demanding (Williams et al., 2014), typically involving complex high speed manoeuvres (Van Damme and Van Dooren, 1999; Kane and Zamani, 2014), underpinned by apparently complicated behavioural options for both predators and prey (Estes and Goddard, 1967; Wilson et al., 2013b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Estes and Goddard (1967) and Wilson et al. (2013b).

claim: Operating in a planar terrestrial environment, options for both predators and prey are restricted, being based primarily on the choice of speed and/or trajectory.
source: In fact, operating in a planar terrestrial environment, options for both parties are restricted, being based primarily on the choice of speed (Elliot et al., 1977) and/or trajectory (Howland, 1974), with actual performance in these being determined by physical constraints that determine maximum attainable speed and limits on turn radius as a function of velocity.
evidence: Supported by citations to Elliot et al. (1977) and Howland (1974).

claim: Actual performance in speed and trajectory is determined by physical constraints that determine maximum attainable speed and limits on turn radius as a function of velocity.
source: In fact, operating in a planar terrestrial environment, options for both parties are restricted, being based primarily on the choice of speed (Elliot et al., 1977) and/or trajectory (Howland, 1974), with actual performance in these being determined by physical constraints that determine maximum attainable speed and limits on turn radius as a function of velocity.
evidence: Based on logical inference from physical principles.

claim: Maximum speed in terrestrial running animals tends to increase to an asymptote with body mass.
source: Maximum speed in terrestrial running animals tends to increase to an asymptote with body mass (Garland, 1983) and this process is driven by increases in leg length with body size, which facilitates higher speeds (Garland, 1983; Bejan and Marden, 2006), being ultimately limited by the scaling of body mass relative to leg strength (Alexander, 2002b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garland (1983).

claim: The increase in maximum speed with body mass is driven by increases in leg length with body size, which facilitates higher speeds.
source: Maximum speed in terrestrial running animals tends to increase to an asymptote with body mass (Garland, 1983) and this process is driven by increases in leg length with body size, which facilitates higher speeds (Garland, 1983; Bejan and Marden, 2006), being ultimately limited by the scaling of body mass relative to leg strength (Alexander, 2002b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garland (1983) and Bejan and Marden (2006).

claim: Maximum speed is ultimately limited by the scaling of body mass relative to leg strength.
source: Maximum speed in terrestrial running animals tends to increase to an asymptote with body mass (Garland, 1983) and this process is driven by increases in leg length with body size, which facilitates higher speeds (Garland, 1983; Bejan and Marden, 2006), being ultimately limited by the scaling of body mass relative to leg strength (Alexander, 2002b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alexander (2002b).

claim: Turn radius as a function of velocity in terrestrial animals is modulated by the extent to which leg strength can support the forces required to generate the centripetal acceleration for the turn.
source: Turn radius as a function of velocity in terrestrial animals is modulated by a number of critical elements, notably the extent to which leg strength can support the forces required to generate the centripetal acceleration for the turn (Greene and McMahon, 1979; Greene, 1985; Alexander, 2002b; Tan and Wilson, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Greene and McMahon (1979), Greene (1985), Alexander (2002b), and Tan and Wilson (2011).

claim: Important elements influencing turning mechanics and maximum turn speed include the interplay of limb force limits and friction limits, and morphological factors.
source: In addition, important elements influencing turning mechanics and maximum turn speed are; the interplay of limb force limits (Chang and Kram, 2007) and friction limits (Usherwood and Wilson, 2005, 2006), and morphological factors (Walter, 2003; Jindrich et al., 2007; Jindrich and Qiao, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chang and Kram (2007), Usherwood and Wilson (2005, 2006), Walter (2003), Jindrich et al. (2007), and Jindrich and Qiao (2009).

claim: The most consistent factor limiting speed during turns in terrestrial animals is force limits.
source: Across these studies on terrestrial animals, however, the most consistent factor limiting speed during turns is force limits, with the total force demands relating to the combined effects of supporting the body mass and providing the necessary acceleration.
evidence: Based on synthesis of multiple studies on terrestrial animal turning.

claim: Total force demands during turns relate to the combined effects of supporting the body mass and providing the necessary acceleration.
source: Across these studies on terrestrial animals, however, the most consistent factor limiting speed during turns is force limits, with the total force demands relating to the combined effects of supporting the body mass and providing the necessary acceleration.
evidence: Based on physical principles of forces during turning.

claim: There must be a broad scaling trend in turning performance with body mass.
source: This means that there must be a broad scaling trend in turning performance with body mass.
evidence: Inferred from the relationship between force demands and body mass.

claim: Such scaling trends in turning performance with body mass have been considered for animals operating in water and air.
source: To our knowledge though, although such scaling trends have been considered for animals operating in water and air (Domenici, 2001; Hedenström and Rosén, 2001), this has not been explicitly examined in the literature for terrestrial animals.
evidence: Supported by citations to Domenici (2001) and Hedenström and Rosén (2001).

claim: Scaling trends in turning performance with body mass have not been explicitly examined in the literature for terrestrial animals.
source: To our knowledge though, although such scaling trends have been considered for animals operating in water and air (Domenici, 2001; Hedenström and Rosén, 2001), this has not been explicitly examined in the literature for terrestrial animals.
evidence: Based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: The scaling trend in turning performance is due to the mismatch between the linear relationship of increased force demands with body size (proportional to Mass^1.0) and the non-linear scaling of leg strength (roughly proportional to Mass^0.66).
source: This trend is due to the mismatch between the linear relationship of increased force demands with body size (proportional to Mass1.0), and the non-linear scaling of leg strength (roughly proportional to Mass0.66 (Schmidt-Nielsen, 1984) (but see Biewener, 1989), leading to a relative decrease in strength, and therefore turn capacity, with increasing size.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmidt-Nielsen (1984) and Biewener (1989).

claim: The mismatch between force demands and leg strength scaling leads to a relative decrease in strength, and therefore turn capacity, with increasing size.
source: This trend is due to the mismatch between the linear relationship of increased force demands with body size (proportional to Mass1.0), and the non-linear scaling of leg strength (roughly proportional to Mass0.66 (Schmidt-Nielsen, 1984) (but see Biewener, 1989), leading to a relative decrease in strength, and therefore turn capacity, with increasing size.
evidence: Inferred from the scaling relationships of force demands and leg strength.

claim: Seminal work on turn performance has essentially concentrated on individual species, where variation with mass is of little consequence except in an absolute sense.
source: The seminal work on turn performance (Greene and McMahon, 1979; Greene, 1985; Usherwood and Wilson, 2005, 2006; Tan and Wilson, 2011) has, to date, essentially concentrated on individual species, where variation with mass is of little consequence except in an absolute sense.
evidence: Based on assessment of cited literature on turn performance.

claim: Where species interact, the mismatch in force scaling would be expected to have profound implications, particularly in predator-prey interactions during pursuit.
source: However, where species interact, we would expect this mismatch to have profound implications, and perhaps nowhere more than in predator-prey interactions during pursuit.
evidence: Inferred from the scaling relationships and their implications for interacting species.

claim: This work investigates the implications of mass in modulating options for terrestrial mammalian predators during the attack phase of attempts at prey capture.
source: This work investigates the implications of mass in modulating options for terrestrial mammalian predators during the attack phase of attempts at prey capture.
evidence: Direct statement of the study's objective.

claim: The study limits itself to terrestrial predation because mass effects have already been examined for organisms in fluid media.
source: We limit ourselves to terrestrial predation because mass effects have already been examined for organisms in fluid media (Domenici, 2001; Van den Hout et al., 2010) and because dealing with animals that operate in a 2-dimensional surface obviates many of the complexities associated with the energetics of changing height in aerial animals (Weihs and Webb, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to Domenici (2001) and Van den Hout et al. (2010).

claim: Dealing with animals that operate in a 2-dimensional surface obviates many of the complexities associated with the energetics of changing height in aerial animals.
source: We limit ourselves to terrestrial predation because mass effects have already been examined for organisms in fluid media (Domenici, 2001; Van den Hout et al., 2010) and because dealing with animals that operate in a 2-dimensional surface obviates many of the complexities associated with the energetics of changing height in aerial animals (Weihs and Webb, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weihs and Webb (1984).

claim: The model assumes that both predators and prey are geometrically similar.
source: Thus, we assume, among other things, that both predators and prey are geometrically similar (which ignores compensating mechanisms such as upright posture and more robust limbs of some large animals as well as variation in traction) and that the chase environment is flat, open and homogeneous (Howland, 1974; Wilson et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated as an assumption of the model.

claim: The model assumes that the chase environment is flat, open and homogeneous.
source: Thus, we assume, among other things, that both predators and prey are geometrically similar (which ignores compensating mechanisms such as upright posture and more robust limbs of some large animals as well as variation in traction) and that the chase environment is flat, open and homogeneous (Howland, 1974; Wilson et al., 2011).
evidence: Stated as an assumption of the model, supported by citations to Howland (1974) and Wilson et al. (2011).

claim: The attack phase of pursuit predators is essentially what has been treated within theory encompassing the 'homicidal chauffeur' game.
source: We propose that the attack phase of pursuit predators is essentially what has been treated within theory encompassing the 'homicidal chauffeur' game (Marec and Van Nhan, 1977), where a car driver attempts to hit a pedestrian in a defined open space.
evidence: Supported by citation to Marec and Van Nhan (1977).

claim: The 'homicidal chauffeur' game involves a car driver attempting to hit a pedestrian in a defined open space.
source: We propose that the attack phase of pursuit predators is essentially what has been treated within theory encompassing the 'homicidal chauffeur' game (Marec and Van Nhan, 1977), where a car driver attempts to hit a pedestrian in a defined open space.
evidence: Supported by citation to Marec and Van Nhan (1977).

claim: Predators should attempt to minimize their distance to the prey.
source: In this, we divide trajectories of both parties into straight line and turn sections and, by adopting a game theory-based approach (Dugatkin and Reeve, 1998; Lima, 2002), we distil out simple objectives for both parties; predators should attempt to minimize their distance to the prey, while prey attempt to maximize this distance (Weihs and Webb, 1984).
evidence: Based on game theory approach, supported by citations to Dugatkin and Reeve (1998), Lima (2002), and Weihs and Webb (1984).

claim: Prey should attempt to maximize their distance from the predator.
source: In this, we divide trajectories of both parties into straight line and turn sections and, by adopting a game theory-based approach (Dugatkin and Reeve, 1998; Lima, 2002), we distil out simple objectives for both parties; predators should attempt to minimize their distance to the prey, while prey attempt to maximize this distance (Weihs and Webb, 1984).
evidence: Based on game theory approach, supported by citations to Dugatkin and Reeve (1998), Lima (2002), and Weihs and Webb (1984).

claim: The most notable attempt to define the predator-prey chase scenario is the work by Howland (1974).
source: To date, the most notable attempt to define the predator-prey chase scenario is the work by Howland (1974), who defined many of the rules and consequences for a single turn gambit and we use this work as a starting point.
evidence: Supported by citation to Howland (1974).

claim: Howland (1974) defined many of the rules and consequences for a single turn gambit.
source: To date, the most notable attempt to define the predator-prey chase scenario is the work by Howland (1974), who defined many of the rules and consequences for a single turn gambit and we use this work as a starting point.
evidence: Supported by citation to Howland (1974).

claim: A large body of theory exists dealing with the best strategy for missiles to engage with their targets to maximize strike probability.
source: However, a large body of theory also exists (notably Wei et al., 2009 and references therein), particularly that dealing with the best strategy for missiles to engage with their targets to maximize strike probability (Shneydor, 1998; Siouris, 2004) and this is also considered within our terrestrial pursuit scenario.
evidence: Supported by citations to Wei et al. (2009), Shneydor (1998), and Siouris (2004).

claim: Single turns initiated by the prey lead to one of primarily two phenomena: either the predator cuts the corner, reducing the predator-prey distance, or it overshoots the corner, increasing the predator-prey distance.
source: Our model for deriving the characteristics of a defined turn as a function of speed in equivalent-sized predators and prey predicted that single turns initiated by the prey lead to one of primarily two phenomena: Either the predator cuts the corner, reducing the predator-prey distance (Figure 1A) benefitting the predator, or it overshoots the corner, increasing the predator-prey distance (Figure 1B) benefitting the prey.
evidence: Predicted by the model and illustrated in Figures 1A and 1B.

claim: A third scenario is where the predator follows the prey trajectory precisely, in which case there is no change in benefit to either party although the predator, with its higher speed, will eventually converge on the prey.
source: A third scenario might be where the predator follows the prey trajectory precisely, in which case there is no change in benefit to either party although in this circumstance, the predator, with its higher speed, will eventually converge on the prey (Figure 1C).
evidence: Predicted by the model and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Multiple turns with consistent undershooting by the predator can lead to capture.
source: Although a single turn may not lead to capture or escape of the prey, multiple turns with consistent undershooting by the predator can do so (Figure 1).
evidence: Predicted by the model and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The change in predator-prey distance over time is critically dependent on the distance between the parties at the moment of the turn, with shorter distances (for distances >0) at the moment of the turn leading to greater overshoot by the predator.
source: For any given turn, the change in predator-prey distance over time was predicted to be critically dependent on; (i) the distance between the parties at the moment of the turn (Figure 2A), with shorter distances (for distances >0) at the moment of the turn leading to greater overshoot by the predator
evidence: Predicted by the model and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The change in predator-prey distance over time is critically dependent on the difference in speed between parties, with greater speed differences leading to greater overshoot by the predator.
source: (ii) the difference in speed between parties (Figure 2B), with greater speed differences leading to greater overshoot by the predator
evidence: Predicted by the model and illustrated in Figure 2B.

claim: The change in predator-prey distance over time is critically dependent on the reaction time of the predator, with slower reaction times leading to greater overshoot.
source: (iii) the reaction time of the predator (Figure 2C), with slower reaction times leading to greater overshoot.
evidence: Predicted by the model and illustrated in Figure 2C.

claim: Where predators and prey have different masses, the model predicted mass-dependent distances travelled in a given turn, with larger animals having to run farther during cornering.
source: Where predators and prey have different masses, the model predicted mass-dependent distances travelled in a given turn, with larger animals having to run farther during cornering (Figure 3).
evidence: Predicted by the model and illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: During a single 90° turn, a 250 kg predator is predicted to have to run farther than all considered prey (potential prey ranging between 3 kg and 200 kg).
source: Thus, during a single 90° turn, a 250 kg predator (an example of which may be a lion or tiger) is predicted to have to run farther than all considered prey (potential prey ranging between a 3 kg and a 200 kg)
evidence: Predicted by the model for specific mass values.

claim: During a single 90° turn, a 30 kg predator is predicted to travel shorter distances during a turn than 3 of the 5 prey masses considered.
source: whereas a 30 kg predator (e.g., a cheetah or a wolf) is predicted to travel shorter distances during a turn than 3 of the 5 prey masses considered (Figure 3).
evidence: Predicted by the model and illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: Cornering is predicted to be more advantageous as an escape manoeuvre as the prey size decreases relative to that of the predator.
source: Thus, cornering is predicted to be more advantageous as an escape manoeuvre as the prey size decreases relative to that of the predator and we would expect to see evidence of that in wild animal data.
evidence: Inferred from the model predictions.

claim: 36 pursuits involving 7 prey species were observed in free-living cheetahs.
source: This prediction could be examined in the data derived from the fieldwork on free-living cheetahs, where we observed 36 pursuits involving 7 prey species (Table 1), of which 33 had corresponding acceleration data for 5 species totalling 899 s.
evidence: Data collected from field observations.

claim: 33 pursuits had corresponding acceleration data for 5 species totalling 899 s.
source: This prediction could be examined in the data derived from the fieldwork on free-living cheetahs, where we observed 36 pursuits involving 7 prey species (Table 1), of which 33 had corresponding acceleration data for 5 species totalling 899 s.
evidence: Data collected from field observations.

claim: A total of 547 turns were documented within all chases from all animals.
source: Identifying cornering behaviour via lateral g-forces, we documented a total of 547 turns within all chases from all animals.
evidence: Data collected from accelerometer measurements.

claim: There was a significant interaction between prey species and turn number on the rate of turn.
source: In these, there was a significant interaction between prey species and turn number (turns were sequentially numbered within each chase) on the rate of turn: specifically, different prey species had different turn rates as the turn numbers progressed (Figure 4) (χ2 = 11.13, p = 0.03, df = 4) (Table 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis of field data (χ2 = 11.13, p = 0.03, df = 4).

claim: Different prey species had different turn rates as the turn numbers progressed.
source: In these, there was a significant interaction between prey species and turn number (turns were sequentially numbered within each chase) on the rate of turn: specifically, different prey species had different turn rates as the turn numbers progressed (Figure 4) (χ2 = 11.13, p = 0.03, df = 4) (Table 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis of field data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: Cheetah turns became shorter as the chase progressed.
source: We also noted that cheetah turns became shorter as the chase progressed (Spearman's ρ = −0.347, p < 0.0001, although g-values reached during turns did not change significantly over time (ρ = 0.031, p = 0.72).
evidence: Statistical analysis of field data (Spearman's ρ = −0.347, p < 0.0001).

claim: G-values reached during turns did not change significantly over time.
source: We also noted that cheetah turns became shorter as the chase progressed (Spearman's ρ = −0.347, p < 0.0001, although g-values reached during turns did not change significantly over time (ρ = 0.031, p = 0.72).
evidence: Statistical analysis of field data (ρ = 0.031, p = 0.72).

claim: Turn dynamics were different in successful and unsuccessful pursuits.
source: Critically, these dynamics were different in successful and unsuccessful pursuits.
evidence: Observed from field data analysis.

claim: Turn duration decreased with increasing turn number within any particular chase.
source: Turn duration decreased with increasing turn number within any particular chase (χ2 = 26.52, df = 1, p < 0.0001)
evidence: Statistical analysis of field data (χ2 = 26.52, df = 1, p < 0.0001).

claim: Turn durations were shorter in successful pursuits.
source: and turn durations were shorter in successful pursuits (χ2 = 6.24, df = 1, p = 0.013).
evidence: Statistical analysis of field data (χ2 = 6.24, df = 1, p = 0.013).

claim: Within the animal mass range considered, mass affects maximum speed (by a factor of less than 6) much less than it affects minimum turning radius at maximum speed (which affects it by a factor of up to 260).
source: Extending our modelling exercise to derive maximum cornering ability as a function of mass and speed for a suite of theoretical mammalian cursorial predators and their prey indicated that, within the animal mass range considered, mass affects maximum speed (by a factor of less than 6) much less than it affects minimum turning radius at maximum speed (which affects it by a factor of up to 260).
evidence: Derived from model calculations.

claim: The differential effect of mass on speed versus turning radius is due to the combined effect of generally increasing maximum speeds with mass and the additional effect of mass on turn radius.
source: This is due to the combined effect of generally increasing maximum speeds with mass (see above) and the additional effect of mass on turn radius (Figure 5).
evidence: Inferred from model results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The surface describing comparative turn abilities showed that predators turn tighter relative to prey in a specific area of the surface defined in terms of predator and prey mass ratios.
source: Importantly though, the surface describing comparative turn abilities showed that predators turn tighter relative to prey in a specific area of the surface defined in terms of predator and prey mass ratios (Figure 5).
evidence: Shown by model results in Figure 5.

claim: All predators from the database were located in the area where predator turn capabilities were maximized compared to their prey.
source: Insertion of the mean mass of 54 species of canids and felids and their (predominantly mammalian) prey from an extensive database (Carbone et al., 1999) into this plot, shows that all predators were located in the area where predator turn capabilities were maximized compared to their prey (Figure 5).
evidence: Data from Carbone et al. (1999) plotted on model predictions in Figure 5.

claim: There is strong selection pressure for turning ability in predators.
source: The implication from this is that there is strong selection pressure for turning ability in predators and that (i) predators evolve to take particular sized prey with a mass that results in the minimum turn radius ratio most in favour of the predator, and/or (ii) prey sizes that have minimum turn radii that most closely accord with those of the predators tend to be caught more often than other-sized prey.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of predator-prey mass ratios observed in the data.

claim: Predators evolve to take particular sized prey with a mass that results in the minimum turn radius ratio most in favour of the predator.
source: The implication from this is that there is strong selection pressure for turning ability in predators and that (i) predators evolve to take particular sized prey with a mass that results in the minimum turn radius ratio most in favour of the predator, and/or (ii) prey sizes that have minimum turn radii that most closely accord with those of the predators tend to be caught more often than other-sized prey.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of predator-prey mass ratios observed in the data.

claim: Prey sizes that have minimum turn radii that most closely accord with those of the predators tend to be caught more often than other-sized prey.
source: The implication from this is that there is strong selection pressure for turning ability in predators and that (i) predators evolve to take particular sized prey with a mass that results in the minimum turn radius ratio most in favour of the predator, and/or (ii) prey sizes that have minimum turn radii that most closely accord with those of the predators tend to be caught more often than other-sized prey.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of predator-prey mass ratios observed in the data.

claim: High speed increases the likelihood that the predator will overshoot the prey turn trajectory.
source: The outcome of a predator-prey pursuit depends on performance, both in terms of speed and cornering capacity (Wilson et al., 2013a, 2013b), and how these relate to power requirements and timing. Our work echoes that of Howland (1974), which dealt with the same issue using a different approach, emphasising that high speed, aside from being necessary for the predator to gain on the prey, also increases the likelihood that the predator will overshoot the prey turn trajectory (Figure 1B) (Howland, 1974; Alexander, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Howland (1974) and Alexander (2003), and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: As speed decreases, the difference in distance covered during any turn between predator and prey decreases.
source: Conversely, as speed decreases, the difference in distance covered during any turn between predator and prey decreases (Figures 1–3), fulfilling the fundamental game rule for the predator.
evidence: Shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: The optimum strategy for a pursuit predator should be to attempt to elicit turns by the prey which, if the prey are working close to maximum power, will result in a reduction in their speed.
source: The optimum strategy for a pursuit predator should, therefore, be to attempt to elicit turns by the prey which, if the prey are working close to maximum power, will result in a reduction in their speed (Shubkina et al., 2012), because energy is needed for the turn (Wilson et al., 2013c).
evidence: Inferred from model predictions and supported by citations to Shubkina et al. (2012) and Wilson et al. (2013c).

claim: Invoking multiple rapid turns might be a strategy that predators seek to promote.
source: Invoking multiple rapid turns might therefore be a strategy that predators seek to promote.
evidence: Inferred from the energetic costs of turning for prey.

claim: Decreasing turn duration over time is expected during successful chases.
source: Here, decreasing turn duration over time is expected during successful chases, as we observed (Figure 4), coupled with generally decreasing speed, as reported by Wilson et al. (Wilson et al., 2013b).
evidence: Predicted by the model and observed in field data shown in Figure 4, supported by citation to Wilson et al. (2013b).

claim: Turning is critical for survival of prey because maintenance of a straight line trajectory leads to inevitable capture if the predator is faster.
source: However, turning is also critical for survival of prey because maintenance of a straight line trajectory leads to inevitable capture if the predator is faster.
evidence: Logical inference from the predator being faster than prey.

claim: When the predator is far from the prey, the prey should not turn since to do so allows the predator to cut the corner of the prey's trajectory and decrease the distance between itself and the prey more rapidly.
source: This seemingly contradictory situation of whether the predators or prey benefit most from prey turns is clarified by timing. When the predator is far from the prey, the prey should not turn since to do so allows the predator to cut the corner of the prey's trajectory and decrease the distance between itself and the prey more rapidly (Eilam, 2005) (Figure 1).
evidence: Inferred from model predictions, supported by citation to Eilam (2005) and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Turns by the prey benefit the prey if the timing is correct because this leads to an overshoot by the predator.
source: However, turns by the prey do benefit the prey if the timing is correct because this leads to an overshoot by the predator (Figure 1, Figure 2).
evidence: Shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Where overshoot turns are consistent, they should generally lead to rarefying turn rates with reduced chances of capture.
source: Where such overshoot turns are consistent, they should generally lead to rarefying turn rates with reduced chances of capture (Wilson et al., 2013b).
evidence: Inferred from model predictions and supported by citation to Wilson et al. (2013b).

claim: The outcome of extended pursuits is likely influenced by endurance.
source: The outcome of extended pursuits is also likely influenced by endurance.
evidence: Logical inference from the energetic demands of extended pursuits.

claim: Both predators and prey have power limitations restricting their options on instantaneous performance and limiting how long the chase can continue before exhaustion.
source: Both parties will have power limitations restricting their options on instantaneous performance, as well as ultimately limiting how long the chase can continue before exhaustion.
evidence: Based on general knowledge of animal physiology.

claim: A multiple turn terrestrial chase has energetic costs associated with straight line travel that are a (linear) function of speed.
source: A multiple turn terrestrial chase has energetic costs associated with straight line travel that are a (linear) function of speed (Taylor and Heglund, 1982)
evidence: Supported by citation to Taylor and Heglund (1982).

claim: There are substantial costs to turning above those of straight line travel.
source: However, there are substantial costs to turning above those of straight line travel (Wilson et al., 2013c)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wilson et al. (2013c).

claim: Where the predator cuts the corner compared to the trajectory taken by the prey, the reduced turn costs should act to reduce its overall rate of energy expenditure, making the predator energy expenditure closer to that of the prey.
source: Thus, where the predator cuts the corner compared to the trajectory taken by the prey (Figure 1), the reduced turn costs should act to reduce its overall rate of energy expenditure, making the predator energy expenditure closer to that of the prey.
evidence: Inferred from the energetic costs of turning and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Where corner-cutting occurs, similarity in power use between parties will tend to lead to similar giving-up times, assuming both parties can allocate similar amounts of energy to a pursuit.
source: This will tend to lead to similarity in power use between parties resulting in similar giving-up times, assuming both parties can allocate similar amounts of energy to a pursuit (Figure 6).
evidence: Inferred from energetic considerations and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Where a predator overshoots the cornering trajectory of the prey, it has to contend with the increased energetic demands of travelling farther, and with a greater turn angle, than the prey.
source: However, where a predator overshoots the cornering trajectory of the prey (Figure 1), it has to contend with the increased energetic demands of travelling farther, and with a greater turn angle, than the prey (Figure 2).
evidence: Inferred from geometric and energetic considerations, illustrated in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Where overshooting occurs consistently, it will tend to make cumulative energy expenditure between the two parties more disparate resulting in the predator reaching endurance limits earlier than the prey.
source: Thus, where overshooting occurs consistently, it will tend to make cumulative energy expenditure between the two parties more disparate resulting in the predator reaching endurance limits earlier than the prey (Figure 6).
evidence: Inferred from energetic considerations and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Multiple turn pursuits will consist of both corner-cutting and overshooting by the predators with the proportion of either perhaps biasing the likelihood of prey capture or the chase being abandoned.
source: In reality, multiple turn pursuits, such as we observed in our cheetah-prey interactions, will consist of a both corner-cutting and overshooting by the predators with the proportion of either perhaps biasing the likelihood of prey capture or the chase being abandoned.
evidence: Inferred from field observations and model predictions.

claim: Mass drives physical abilities in predator-prey pursuits.
source: Our data and theoretical considerations based on the literature highlight the extent to which mass drives physical abilities in predator-prey pursuits.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from data and model results.

claim: The fact that maximum speed generally increases with mass has been variously linked to factors such as absolute and relative leg length, stride length and stride frequency.
source: The fact that maximum speed generally increases with mass (Garland, 1983) has been variously linked to factors such as absolute and relative leg length, stride length and stride frequency (cf. Schmidt-Nielsen, 1984; Biewener, 1989, 2003; Alexander, 2002a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Garland (1983), Schmidt-Nielsen (1984), Biewener (1989, 2003), and Alexander (2002a).

claim: Greater mass leads to greater turn radii because the forces that animals can exert for a turn relate to a mass exponent of less than one, whereas the forces required for a turn scale to a mass exponent of one.
source: That greater mass leads to greater turn radii, because the forces that animals can exert for a turn relate to a mass exponent of less than one, whereas the forces required for a turn scale to a mass exponent of one has not, to our knowledge, been previously discussed.
evidence: Based on scaling principles and the authors' assessment that this has not been previously discussed.

claim: Both mass-dependent attributes (speed and turn radius) lead to a tendency for larger animals to be faster, but less able to turn than smaller animals.
source: Both these mass-dependent attributes lead to a tendency for larger animals to be faster, but less able to turn than smaller animals, which presumably has profound consequences for strategies adopted by predators and prey during pursuits.
evidence: Inferred from the scaling relationships of speed and turn radius with mass.

claim: Mass-linked performance explains why smaller cheetah prey confer a greater size-derived speed advantage to the predator, which should lead to a more rapid closure of the cheetah-prey distance during straight line sections of the pursuit and result in a predicted, and observed, higher turning frequency in cheetah pursuing smaller prey.
source: Mass-linked performance explains why, for example, smaller cheetah prey confer a greater size-derived speed advantage to the predator, which should lead to a more rapid closure of the cheetah-prey distance during straight line sections of the pursuit and result in a predicted, and observed, higher turning frequency in cheetah pursuing smaller prey (Figure 4, Table 1).
evidence: Inferred from model predictions and confirmed by field data shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: The mass-dependent model of performance points to how predator size in relation to that of the prey results in differential distances travelled by both parties during turns.
source: Similarly, our mass-dependent model of performance points to how predator size in relation to that of the prey results in differential distances travelled by both parties during turns.
evidence: Derived from model predictions.

claim: The distance run during any given turn by a predator with similar mass to its prey should not be markedly greater than its prey, while a larger predator chasing the same prey must contend with covering a substantial increase in the distance travelled.
source: So the distance run during any given turn by a predator with similar mass to its prey should not be markedly greater than its prey, while a larger predator chasing the same prey must contend with covering a substantial increase in the distance travelled (Figure 3).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3.

claim: Either party may elect to travel more slowly to produce a tighter turning radius, which also reduces the chances of mistakes.
source: However, the scaling of turning radius with speed is complex because either party may elect to travel more slowly to produce a tighter turning radius, which also reduces the chances of mistakes (Chittka et al., 2009), although the predator must always presumably travel faster than the prey.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chittka et al. (2009).

claim: Workers have suggested and found that cheetahs tend to reduce speed in the final stages of their chases.
source: Certainly, workers have suggested (Wilson et al., 2013a), and found (Wilson et al., 2013b), that cheetahs tend to reduce speed in the final stages of their chases (cf. Shubkina et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wilson et al. (2013a, 2013b) and Shubkina et al. (2012).

claim: Varying masses between predators and prey changes the nature of pursuits substantially.
source: Thus, varying masses between predators and prey changes the nature of pursuits substantially.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from model predictions and field data.

claim: Pursuit predators up to body masses of about 70 kg would seem to need to be larger than their prey in order to be able to catch them because, up to this size, larger animals can run faster.
source: Pursuit predators up to body masses of about 70 kg would seem to need to be larger than their prey in order to be able to catch them because, up to this size, larger animals can run faster (Garland, 1983; Bejan and Marden, 2006).
evidence: Inferred from the speed-mass relationship, supported by citations to Garland (1983) and Bejan and Marden (2006).

claim: Larger-bodied predators must modulate speed carefully to compensate for their turn radius disadvantages because, although they can outrun, they are less likely to out-manoeuvre their prey.
source: But larger-bodied predators must modulate speed carefully to compensate for their turn radius disadvantages because, although they can outrun, they are less likely to out-manoeuvre their prey (Figures 3, 4).
evidence: Inferred from model predictions shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Chases are expected to be defined by more frequent turns with increasing mass differential between parties.
source: Therefore, chases are expected to be defined by more frequent turns with increasing mass differential between parties, which is what we observed in our cheetah data (Table 1).
evidence: Predicted by the model and confirmed by field data in Table 1.

claim: Where predators pursue prey larger than themselves, and assuming that the predator can travel faster than their prey, there is no advantage to be gained by the prey executing the sudden turns characteristic of small prey.
source: Where predators pursue prey larger than themselves, however, and assuming that the predator can travel faster than their prey, there is no advantage to be gained by the prey executing the sudden turns characteristic of small prey (cf. Figure 4).
evidence: Inferred from model predictions and referenced to Figure 4.

claim: The straight-line trajectories of gemsbok being pursued by spotted hyaenas are explained by the lack of turning advantage for larger prey.
source: This explains the straight-line trajectories of for example, gemsbok Oryx gazelle being pursued by spotted hyaenas Crocuta crocuta (Mills, 1990).
evidence: Inferred from model predictions and supported by citation to Mills (1990).

claim: The primary deterrent to smaller predators hunting larger animals may come from the danger of injury or the predator not having the strength to overcome its prey.
source: The primary deterrent to smaller predators hunting larger animals may come from the danger of injury (Mills, 1990), or the predator not having the strength to overcome its prey, something that can be mitigated to an extent by co-operative hunting or following the prey to exhaustion (Estes and Goddard, 1967).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mills (1990) and Estes and Goddard (1967).

claim: Variation in the topography and vegetation is expected to modulate the tactics adopted by both predators and prey.
source: Our treatise assumes that both predators and prey interact on a homogeneous, flat surface but we expect any variation in the topography and vegetation to modulate the tactics adopted by both predators and prey.
evidence: Logical inference from environmental heterogeneity.

claim: Substrate type affects the costs of animals moving over it, which is predicted to affect route choice in a general sense.
source: Shepard et al., (2013) note how substrate type affects the costs of animals moving over it (hence their term 'energy landscape'), which is predicted to affect route choice in a general sense.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shepard et al. (2013).

claim: High power pursuits are expected to be subject to the same rules as general movement, with changes in the energy landscape that differentially affect predators and their prey to be exploited by the relevant party.
source: We expect high power pursuits of the type discussed here to be subject to the same rules, with changes in the energy landscape that differentially affect predators and their prey to be exploited by the relevant party.
evidence: Inferred from the energy landscape concept.

claim: Larger animals incur a proportionately greater increase in metabolic rate for movement up inclines.
source: Of particular note is the work by Taylor et al., (1972), who noted that larger animals incur a proportionately greater increase in metabolic rate for movement up inclines, and this has been shown to affect area use in some species (Wall et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Taylor et al. (1972) and Wall et al. (2006).

claim: Smaller prey are expected to favour selection of uphill gradients during pursuits.
source: Correspondingly, we would expect smaller prey to favour selection of uphill gradients during pursuits.
evidence: Inferred from the differential energetic costs of uphill movement for different sized animals.

claim: Smaller prey are expected to 'run for cover' partly because such cover may represent an impossibly high-cost energy landscape for the predators.
source: Similarly, smaller prey are expected to 'run for cover' (Domenici et al., 2011), partly because such cover may represent an impossibly high-cost energy landscape for the predators.
evidence: Inferred from energy landscape considerations and supported by citation to Domenici et al. (2011).

claim: Vegetation in patches may constrain turn radii, precluding small prey from turning as tightly as they might, to the advantage of the predator.
source: In addition, vegetation in patches, such as bushes or trees, may constrain turn radii, precluding small prey from perhaps turning as tightly as they might, to the advantage of the predator
evidence: Inferred from the physical constraints imposed by vegetation.

claim: Environmental features may allow prey to execute a turn without giving the predator the option of cutting the corner.
source: while, conversely, such features may allow prey to execute a turn without giving the predator the option of cutting the corner (Figure 7).
evidence: Illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Some authors have noted that unpredictable (protean) movement by prey can enhance their chances of escape.
source: Within the general context of predator-prey pursuits, some authors have noted that unpredictable (protean) movement by prey can enhance their chances of escape (Jones et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jones et al. (2011).

claim: The theory is that unpredictable movement may catch the predator by surprise.
source: The theory is that unpredictable movement may catch the predator by surprise (Humphries and Driver, 1970), not least because, in our case of cursorial predator-prey interactions, the prey may execute a turn when the predator-prey distance is not yet critical.
evidence: Supported by citation to Humphries and Driver (1970).

claim: In planar environments, choices for changing trajectory can only amount to movement that is either left or right.
source: Clearly, if this occurs in planar environments, choices for changing trajectory can only amount to movement that is either left or right, and should not be executed too early where there are substantial corner-cutting benefits to be gained by the predator.
evidence: Based on geometric constraints of planar movement.

claim: Since the timing of corners appears so critical, selection pressure for random turns just before the critical phase would be expected.
source: However, since the timing of corners would appear so critical (see above), we would expect selection pressure for random turns just before the critical phase.
evidence: Inferred from the importance of timing in turn outcomes.

claim: Predator-prey pursuit options by terrestrial animals will be altered when the condition changes from single to multiple predators.
source: Finally, predator-prey pursuit options by terrestrial animals will undoubtedly be altered when the condition changes from single to multiple predators.
evidence: Logical inference from the change in predator numbers.

claim: Observed manoeuvres in multiple predator scenarios are complex and include fanning out of predators.
source: Here, observed manoeuvres are complex and include fanning out of predators (Kelley, 1973; Mills, 1990) which should allow larger predators to mitigate for the effects of their reduced turning radii with respect to those of their prey.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kelley (1973) and Mills (1990).

claim: Fanning out of predators should allow larger predators to mitigate for the effects of their reduced turning radii with respect to those of their prey.
source: Here, observed manoeuvres are complex and include fanning out of predators (Kelley, 1973; Mills, 1990) which should allow larger predators to mitigate for the effects of their reduced turning radii with respect to those of their prey.
evidence: Inferred from the spatial distribution of multiple predators.

claim: There are different strategies recognised within 'pursuit' scenarios including 'pure' pursuit, 'constant bearing' pursuit, and 'constant absolute target direction' (CATD) pursuit.
source: There are a number of different strategies recognised within 'pursuit' scenarios (e.g., athletes chasing balls, children's games of 'tag', missiles, and insects involved in territorial disputes) including, primarily 'pure' pursuit, and more 'predictive' strategies such as 'constant bearing' pursuit, and 'constant absolute target direction' (CATD) pursuit (for definitions see Shneydor, 1998; Wei et al., 2009; Nahin, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shneydor (1998), Wei et al. (2009), and Nahin (2012).

claim: Constant bearing is only applicable if the speeds of both parties are constant.
source: Constant bearing is only applicable if the speeds of both parties are constant (Reddy, 2007), which is generally inappropriate for predator-prey terrestrial pursuits (Wilson et al., 2013b)
evidence: Supported by citations to Reddy (2007) and Wilson et al. (2013b).

claim: Constant bearing pursuit has been demonstrated in some predatory insects, fish and humans.
source: although its use has been demonstrated in some predatory insects (Olberg et al., 2000), fish (Lanchester and Mark, 1975) and humans (McBeath et al., 1995)
evidence: Supported by citations to Olberg et al. (2000), Lanchester and Mark (1975), and McBeath et al. (1995).

claim: CATD and 'pure pursuit' have been shown in some birds.
source: while CATD has been shown in some birds, as has 'pure pursuit' (Kane et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kane et al. (2015).

claim: Pursuit strategies for flying animals are expected to differ from those of terrestrial animals.
source: We expect, however, pursuit strategies for flying animals (and some latter-day missiles) to differ from those of terrestrial animals.
evidence: Inferred from the differences in operating environments.

claim: Initial engagement between two aerial parties invariably involves both moving prey and the pursuer having an approach that tends to occur at a tangent to the target.
source: This is because initial engagement between two aerial parties invariably involves both moving prey and the pursuer having an approach that tends to occur at a tangent to the target (Hedenström and Rosén, 2001; Ghose et al., 2006), rather than from directly behind.
evidence: Supported by citations to Hedenström and Rosén (2001) and Ghose et al. (2006).

claim: Part of the reason for tangential approach in aerial predators relates to both predators and prey operating in 3-d, rather than 2-d, space so that the simple probability of a line of attack being directly along and behind the prey flight path at first encounter is correspondingly reduced.
source: Part of the reason for this tangent relates to both predators and prey operating in 3-d, rather than 2-d, space so that the simple probability of a line of attack being directly along and behind the prey flight path at first encounter is correspondingly reduced.
evidence: Inferred from geometric considerations in 3-d space.

claim: Tangential approach provides various options for pursuers to calculate trajectories and compute intersection points that minimize time and/or distance.
source: Tangential approach provides various options for pursuers to calculate trajectories and compute intersection points (Olberg et al., 2000) that minimize time and/or distance (Ghose et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Olberg et al. (2000) and Ghose et al. (2006).

claim: Tangential approach helps mitigate manoeuvring problems likely to occur during pure pursuit as the inter-party distance approaches zero.
source: It also helps mitigate manoeuvring problems likely to occur during pure pursuit as the inter-party distance approaches zero (particularly where pursuer speed is much greater than that of the prey) (Siouris, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siouris (2004).

claim: The development of the chase for a cursorial predator operating in the planer environment of the ground invariably starts with a stalking phase on essentially non-moving prey followed by the rush.
source: The development of the chase for a cursorial predator operating in the planer environment of the ground, however, invariably starts with a stalking phase on essentially non-moving prey followed by the rush (Estes and Goddard, 1967; Elliot et al., 1977; Mills, 1990; Williams et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Estes and Goddard (1967), Elliot et al. (1977), Mills (1990), and Williams et al. (2014).

claim: One option for prey escape, more appropriate where the predator speed is markedly higher than prey and the distance between them small, involves prey escaping in a trajectory that is perpendicular to that of the predator.
source: One, which is more appropriate where the predator speed is markedly higher than prey and the distance between them small, involves prey escaping in a trajectory that is perpendicular to that of the predator (Weihs and Webb, 1984; Stankowich and Coss, 2007; Domenici et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Weihs and Webb (1984), Stankowich and Coss (2007), and Domenici et al. (2011).

claim: The 'side step' strategy capitalizes on the speed-linked smaller turn radius of the prey compared to the predator.
source: In part, this 'side step' strategy capitalizes on the speed-linked smaller turn radius of the prey compared to the predator.
evidence: Inferred from the relationship between speed and turn radius.

claim: If prey react to a distant, but approaching, predator by generally moving away, the speeds of both parties will tend to become better matched over time.
source: Otherwise, if prey react to a distant, but approaching, predator by generally moving away, the speeds of both parties will tend to become better matched over time.
evidence: Inferred from the dynamics of pursuit.

claim: When speeds are matched, the best strategy is for prey to continue to move directly away because any other direction will reduce the inter-party distance correspondingly.
source: Here, the best strategy is for prey to continue to move directly away because any other direction will reduce the inter-party distance correspondingly (cf. Domenici et al., 2011).
evidence: Inferred from geometric considerations and supported by citation to Domenici et al. (2011).

claim: Observations report that prey typically do indeed initially run directly away from the predators.
source: This explains observations reporting that prey typically do indeed initially run directly away from the predators (cf. Finney et al., 1997; Broom and Ruxton, 2005; Eilam, 2005) although this is not always the case (see review in Domenici et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Finney et al. (1997), Broom and Ruxton (2005), Eilam (2005), and Domenici et al. (2011).

claim: The manoeuvre of prey running directly away puts the pursuer directly behind the prey.
source: This manoeuvre puts the pursuer directly behind the prey.
evidence: Inferred from the geometry of the escape trajectory.

claim: During the ensuing pursuit phase, straight line pursuit by the predator towards the prey is the only viable predator option when the prey travels in a straight line.
source: During the ensuing pursuit phase, straight line pursuit by the predator towards the prey is the only viable predator option when the prey travels in a straight line (ignoring topographic complexity —see 'Discussion'), which is also what has been observed (Shubkina et al., 2012 and refs therein).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shubkina et al. (2012) and references therein.

claim: As the predator-prey distance tends towards zero, the prey must turn to avoid capture.
source: As the predator-prey distance tends towards zero, the prey must turn to avoid capture, and may even have particular strategies such as stotting to enhance this (Stankowich and Coss, 2007).
evidence: Logical inference from the pursuit dynamics and supported by citation to Stankowich and Coss (2007).

claim: There is considerable selection pressure on the prey to time the turn so that it occurs close to the contact point (but not so close that the predator catches it).
source: We demonstrate later that there is considerable selection pressure on the prey to time this turn so that it occurs close to the contact point (but not so close that the predator catches it).
evidence: Inferred from model predictions presented later in the manuscript.

claim: The scenario of prey turning close to contact reduces differences, in both trajectories and time to contact, between the different pursuit strategies.
source: This scenario reduces differences, in both trajectories and time to contact, between the different pursuit strategies (see above) although any predictive pursuit options typically have a reduced trajectory length and time to contact than pure pursuit (see below).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of pursuit strategies.

claim: Differences between the pursuit strategies are likely reduced by prey reaction to the approaching predator based on the prey having properly informed assessment of predator trajectory.
source: Differences between the pursuit strategies are also likely reduced by prey reaction to the approaching predator based on the prey having properly informed assessment of predator trajectory.
evidence: Inferred from prey sensory capabilities.

claim: Typical terrestrial 'prey', such as ungulates, have large panoramic visual fields with laterally facing orbital margins.
source: In this regard, typical terrestrial 'prey', such as ungulates, have large panoramic visual fields with laterally facing orbital margins (Heesy, 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Heesy (2004).

claim: Prey may be able to assess the movements of their pursuers as well as their pursuers can assess them.
source: and so may be able to assess the movements of their pursuers as well as their pursuers can assess them.
evidence: Inferred from prey visual capabilities.

claim: Escape trajectories may be modulated to keep predators within the prey's visual (or other sensory) fields.
source: Indeed, escape trajectories may be modulated to keep predators within the prey's visual (or other sensory) fields (Domenici et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Domenici et al. (2011).

claim: The substantive differences between terrestrial and fluid media interactions may partly account for the reason that many terrestrial cursorial predators adopt pure pursuit.
source: In any event, the substantive differences between terrestrial and fluid media interactions may partly account for the reason that Shneydor (1998) considers that many terrestrial cursorial predators adopt pure pursuit (hence the name 'hound-hare pursuit'), something that is backed up by observation (Schaller, 2009; Shubkina et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shneydor (1998), Schaller (2009), and Shubkina et al. (2010, 2012).

claim: Quantitative differences in trajectories and pursuit times between pure- and predictive pursuit strategies do not change qualitative patterns.
source: Importantly though, quantitative differences in trajectories and pursuit times between pure- and predictive pursuit strategies do not change qualitative patterns.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of pursuit strategies.

claim: The essential message of the work, which considers mass effects, does not depend on the choice of pursuit strategy.
source: Thus, the essential message of the work, which considers mass effects, does not depend on our choice of pursuit strategy.
evidence: Stated by the authors as a conclusion about their approach.

claim: The model assumes that predator-prey interactions occur in a flat, homogenous area, otherwise lacking physical structure.
source: A. That predator-prey interactions occur in a flat, homogenous area, otherwise lacking physical structure (Marec and Van Nhan, 1977; Melikyan and Bernhard, 2005) and with no differential power requirements according to trajectory direction (Shepard et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as an assumption, supported by citations to Marec and Van Nhan (1977), Melikyan and Bernhard (2005), and Shepard et al. (2013).

claim: The model assumes that only the pursuit phase of a hunting predator is considered.
source: B. That only the pursuit phase of a hunting predator is considered (Elliot et al., 1977).
evidence: Stated as an assumption, supported by citation to Elliot et al. (1977).

claim: The model assumes that distance between predator and prey is chosen as the primary focus, with prey maximizing instantaneous distance.
source: C. That distance between predator and prey is chosen as the primary focus of the model, with prey maximizing instantaneous distance (Weihs and Webb, 1984).
evidence: Stated as an assumption, supported by citation to Weihs and Webb (1984).

claim: The model assumes that both predator and prey are solitary.
source: D. That both predator and prey are solitary.
evidence: Stated as an assumption.

claim: The model assumes that prey operate close to maximizing energy input to locomotion during the chase although the predators are not required to do so.
source: F. That prey operate close to maximizing energy input to locomotion during the chase although the predators are not required to do so.
evidence: Stated as an assumption.

claim: The pursuit is defined as consisting of two fundamental stages: stage 1, which involves straight line travel by the predator towards the prey and straight line travel by the prey in response, and stage 2, where the prey initiates turns to reduce the chances of being caught and the predator responds by turning during pursuit.
source: We define the pursuit as consisting of two fundamental stages; stage 1, which involves straight line travel by the predator towards the prey and, if the prey is not caught immediately, straight line travel by the prey in response to this, and stage 2, where the prey initiates turns to reduce the chances of being caught and the predator responds by turning during pursuit.
evidence: Stated as a definition in the model.

claim: The predator initiates the chase by starting from a concealed position and accelerating towards a stationary or near-stationary prey some distance s away.
source: It is assumed that the predator initiates the chase by starting from a concealed position and accelerating towards a stationary or near-stationary prey some distance s away.
evidence: Stated as an assumption in the model.

claim: The prey does not move in response until the predator approaches within a certain distance x, determined by its ability to sense the predator's approach and its reaction time.
source: The prey does not move in response until the predator approaches within a certain distance x, determined by its ability to sense the predator's approach and its reaction time.
evidence: Stated as an assumption in the model.

claim: The ultimate turning ability of an animal is limited by the mechanical strength of its bones, muscles and tendons since this determines the maximum force available to the animal that can be applied to the ground.
source: Clearly, the ultimate turning ability of an animal is limited by the mechanical strength of its bones, muscles and tendons since this determines the maximum force available to the animal that can be applied to the ground.
evidence: Based on biomechanical principles.

claim: The ultimate compressive strength of compact bone is 170 × 10^6 N/m^2.
source: For example, the ultimate compressive strength of compact bone is 170 × 106 N/m2
evidence: Based on material properties of bone.

claim: The tensile strength of ligament and tendon is 50–100 × 10^6 N/m^2.
source: the tensile strength of ligament and tendon is 50–100 × 106 N/m2
evidence: Based on material properties of ligaments and tendons.

claim: The tensile strength values for muscle are lower, in the range 10^5–10^6 N/m^2.
source: while these values for muscle are lower, in the range 105–106 N/m2.
evidence: Based on material properties of muscle.

claim: Six free-ranging cheetahs in the Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park were equipped with collar-fitted tri-axial accelerometers.
source: We examined the perspectives from our models with respect to prey pursuit behaviour observed directly, and quantified using collar-fitted tri-axial accelerometers (G6a, Cefas, UK —recording rate 30 Hz), on six free-ranging cheetahs in the Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park (25°46′S 20°23′E), southern Africa.
evidence: Description of field methods.

claim: Cheetahs varied in mass between 30 and 45 kg.
source: Cheetahs, which varied in mass between 30 and 45 kg, were equipped for a total of 66 animal days during which 36 pursuits of prey were observed.
evidence: Data from field observations.

claim: Cheetahs were equipped for a total of 66 animal days.
source: Cheetahs, which varied in mass between 30 and 45 kg, were equipped for a total of 66 animal days during which 36 pursuits of prey were observed.
evidence: Data from field observations.

claim: Turns were identified as increasing departures of the doubly smoothed data from 1×g.
source: Turns were identified as increasing departures of the doubly smoothed data from 1×g.
evidence: Description of data analysis method.

claim: Data from an extensive database on the mass of mammalian predators and their mammal prey were used to examine whether the model explains general patterns in prey size selection.
source: We then took data from an extensive data base on the mass of mammalian predators and their mammal prey (Carbone et al., 1999) so as to place data from wild animals in this context to determine whether any trends were apparent.
evidence: Data from Carbone et al. (1999) used for analysis.
